name: Bunan
confidence_why: Widmer 2017, the reference grammar, puts stress on the first syllable of words spoken in isolation (cued by pitch, insensitive to syllable weight, not phonemic, with a second-syllable phrasal stress in connected speech) and explicitly reanalyses the weight-conditioned, partly phonemic accent of Sharma 1989 as tone or phonation, so the answer is clear but rests on only two descriptions that describe different systems.
catalog_citation: Widmer, Manuel. 2014. A descriptive grammar of Bunan. PhD dissertation, Faculty of Humanities, Universität Bern. xxiv+886 pp. [same sec. 2.5.1 text published as Widmer 2017, A Grammar of Bunan (MGL 71), De Gruyter Mouton, ch. 2, DOI 10.1515/9783110766295-006]
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 'Phonetics and Phonology', sec. 2.5 'Suprasegmental features', sec. 2.5.1 'Stress', diss. pp. 117-119 (saved text file; the section continues to p. 130); also sec. 2.5.2 'Phonation' pp. 130-131 (ff.) and sec. 2.6.2 'Prosodic features' p. 133 (ff.)
catalog_quote: Polysyllabic words carry a prominent stress on the first syllable when uttered in isolation. In Bunan, the main correlate of stress is pitch [...] the morphological structure of the word has no effect on the placement of stress. As stress is always assigned to the first syllable of a word, polysyllabic words cannot differ from each other in terms of placement of stress. Consequently, stress is not phonemic in Bunan. [...] The trochaic stress pattern discussed above is, however, only attested at the word level, that is in words that are spoken in isolation. When polysyllabic words are uttered in the context of phrases, they follow an iambic stress pattern that is dictated by phrasal intonation.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: 2.6. Accent. Accent in Gahri is both phonemic and non-phonemic. Though examples of the phonemic constrast of the accent are attested in a few monosyllabic words only, yet it is very much a part of the sound system in it: e.g. /ló/ south: /lo/ age, year /lá/ goat: /la/ moon. Normally, a monosyllabic words is uttered with a prominent stress accent on it, e.g. /la/ goat, /le/ tongue, /phug/ hole, /du/ cloud. /din/ day, etc. In dissyllabic words, however, the prominent accent is on the initial syllable, if it is close and on the second syllable if both the syllables are open, as in /pum-pa/ shoulder, /wam-pu/ a bear, /lag-thil/ palm, but /khyu-či/ arm, /bo-či/ finger, /cáva/ deer, /si-ga/ saddle, /ku-śu/ a kind of apple, /su-gu/ paper, /phe-ce/ uncle. In polysyllabic words all syllables carry a secondary accent only, as in /te-pań-po/ thumb, /co-bo-ci/ index finger, /la-la-ci/ kid, /ka-ka-ci/ lamb. etc. (not marked).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Monosyllables bear a prominent stress accent. In disyllables the prominent accent falls on the first syllable when that syllable is closed, otherwise (both syllables open) on the second syllable. Words of three or more syllables are said to have no single prominent syllable, all syllables carrying only 'secondary accent'. Separately, a marginal lexical accent contrast (acute-marked vs unmarked vowel) distinguishes a few monosyllabic pairs.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Author states that in polysyllabic (3+ syllable) words 'all syllables carry a secondary accent only' (i.e. no primary prominence); not marked in his transcription.
new_statements.exceptions: A few monosyllabic minimal pairs distinguished only by 'accent' (ló 'south' vs lo 'age, year'; lá 'goat' vs la 'moon'), which the author calls phonemic accent; one open-open disyllable is written with an accent on the first vowel (/cáva/ 'deer') without comment. No rule given for closed non-initial syllables or for CVC.CVC words beyond the examples pum-pa, wam-pu, lag-thil (all initial-closed).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern isolated words (elicited citation forms) from two Keylong-area speakers; no discussion of phrase-level prominence or of affixed/polymorphemic words.
new_statements.identity_note: Sharma describes 'Gahri (Bunan/Punan)' of the lower Bhaga (Gahr) valley, Lahaul, from two speakers of Lower Keylong and Upper Keylong-Guskyar; this is the same language as Glottolog gahr1239 Bunan (ISO bfu), no dialect split involved. Note the LSI-Himachal Pradesh 2023 'Lahauli' chapter is Stod Bhoti, not Bunan, and must not be attached to this key.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (world-2026-09-17) has an empty rule; the only existing statement is Sharma 1989 sec. 2.6 'Accent' (read weight-sensitive: disyllables stressed on a closed initial syllable, otherwise on the second syllable; 'phonemic' accent in monosyllabic pairs ló/lo, lá/la). Widmer 2014 differs on every point: (a) isolation-form stress is invariably initial and non-phonemic (Sharma's open-open disyllables like bo-tsi 'finger', ka-ka-tsi 'lamb' would be initial-stressed in isolation for Widmer); (b) the second-syllable prominence Widmer does find is a phrase-level iambic pattern that he states is explicitly NOT sensitive to syllable weight (/ʂaŋs.ˈpa/ keeps second-syllable stress despi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level stress (citation forms, words in isolation): trochaic, always on the first syllable of a polysyllabic word, including compounds (me-ɕiŋ 'firewood'); main acoustic correlate is pitch (higher, level F0 on syllable 1), intensity unreliable; placement never varies, so stress is not phonemic. In connected speech a different, iambic 'phrase-level stress' dictated by phrasal intonation falls on the SECOND syllable of a polysyllabic word regardless of syllable weight (/ʂaŋs.ˈpa/, /ba.ˈjaks/) and regardless of mono- vs polymorphemic status (/lak.ˈgjap/, /te.ˈa.wa/, /al.ˈkjo.tsi/); but it is morphologically conditioned: lexical roots attract it and grammatical suffixes/clitics cannot bear it, so root+grammatical-morpheme words are stressed on the root (/ˈgi=tok/, /ˈkʰet-ø-dza/); nominal derivational -pa, -tsi behave like lexical syllables (ʂaŋs-ˈpa, pel-ˈtsi) while adjectival -na and non-finite verbal endings (-men, -ka, -dʑi) are unstressed. Hence phrasal stress is 'only weakly phonemic', with morphology-driven minimal pairs /mik.ˈti/ 'tear' (eye+water) vs /ˈmik.ti/ 'eye=INDEF'. Sec. 2.6.2 (p. 133): every phonological word bears exactly one primary phrasal stress; first syllable if one monosyllabic lexical root + grammatical material, second syllable if the lexical stem is polysyllabic or there are several lexical stems (aˈtɕʰo, kaˈkatsi, meˈɕiŋ). Sec. 2.5.2 (p. 130): Sharma's (1989b: 202) monosyllabic 'phonemic accent' pairs ló/lo, lá/la 'do not contrast in terms of accent / stress but rather in terms of tone / phonation'; Widmer's elicitation 'confirmed my impression that Bunan is not a tonal language' - the elusive contrast is breathy vs modal voice (la 'goat' vs la̤ 'moon').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Under phrasal (iambic) stress, in the rare quadrisyllabic words 'the fourth syllable tends to be stressed as well. However, this stress is clearly less prominent than the primary stress on the second syllable and sometimes does not occur at all, e.g. /braŋ.ˈsi.bu.(ˌ)jaŋ/ “honey bee”' (p. 120). No secondary stress described for isolation forms.
new_statements.exceptions: Phrasal stress: grammatical morphemes (inflectional suffixes, clitics such as =dzi, =tok, =tiki, -dza) never bear it; derivational suffixes split - nominal -pa (agentive nominalizer) and -tsi (diminutive) are stressable like lexical syllables (explained via Bybee-style 'autonomy', high token frequency, and opaque Tibetan loans in -pa), adjectival -na and non-finite verbal -men/-ka/-dʑi are not; the basic pattern can be overlaid by pragmatic contours such as the clause-final 'non-final rise', which raises pitch on the last syllable whether lexical or grammatical (pp. 127-130). Word-level (isolation) initial stress has no stated exceptions; morphological structure 'has no effect on the placement of stress' there.
new_statements.identity_note: Widmer 2014 describes Bunan (autonym; exonym Gahri) of the Gahr valley, Lahaul (Himachal Pradesh), fieldwork 2010-2014 with speakers TD, NN, SA, TDrol and others; Sharma 1989's 'Gahri' chapter is the same language, so no variety mismatch explains the disagreement. The text read is the December 2014 Bern dissertation (title page present in the embedded text), i.e. the listed item, not the 2017 Mouton Grammar Library 71 revision (whose sec. 2.5.1 'Stress', per the Google Books snippets already held by the project, carries the same analysis).

readall_conflicts: The one listed open work (Widmer 2014) could not be opened, so nothing new was read from the listed works and the catalog's existing statement (Sharma 1989, sec. 2.6 'Accent', p. 202: monosyllables carry a prominent stress accent; in disyllables the accent falls on the initial syllable if it is closed and on the second if both syllables are open; polysyllables carry only secondary accent; a few monosyllabic minimal pairs treated as phonemic accent) stands as recorded, reading weight-sensitive. There is, however, a documented disagreement waiting in the search-snippet evidence material already held by the project from the 2017 Mouton revision of Widmer's grammar (not a listed item, paywalled): Widmer 2017 sec. 2.5.1 states that polysyllabic words carry a prominent stress on the first syllable when uttered in isolation (trochaic, pitch the main correlate), that stress is not phonemic in Bunan (elsewhere 'only weakly phonemic', with a few minimal pairs such as mik-ti 'tear'), that in phrases polysyllabic words follow an iambic phrase-level pattern with phrasal stress on the second lexical syllable of the stem, that this phrasal stress 'is not sensitive to syllable weight', and that Sharma's monosyllabic 'phonemic accent' pairs (ló/lo, lá/la) contrast in tone/phonation rather than stress.
